name: Apache XTable
summary: An incubating Apache project, formerly Onehouse’s OneTable, that makes one set of Parquet files readable as a Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg and Apache Hudi table at once by translating only the table metadata.
intro: Hudi, Iceberg and Delta Lake all keep their data in Parquet files and differ in the metadata on top: Hudi’s timeline, Iceberg’s manifests and Delta’s JSON transaction log. XTable reads the source table’s metadata into a common in-memory model (schema, partitioning, the list of data files with their column statistics, row counts and sizes) and writes the same table out in each target format’s metadata, next to the source’s, in the same directory. No data file is copied or rewritten. A sync runs in “incremental” mode, which replays only the commits since the last sync, and falls back to a “full” snapshot sync when incremental isn’t safe. It also maintains the target metadata: it marks files as cleaned for Hudi, expires old Iceberg snapshots and retains Delta’s log for a set time. Since 0.3.0 it can also register the result in Hive Metastore or AWS Glue.

Sources are Hudi, Iceberg and Delta, plus, since 0.4.0 (August 2026), Apache Paimon and plain Parquet directories. Targets are Hudi, Iceberg, Delta and a Delta Kernel writer. You run it as the `RunSync` utility, a bundled jar that you build yourself with Java 11 and Maven, because Apache releases are source-only, or as `xtable-spark-runtime`, a 4 MB jar on Maven Central for Spark 3.4 and 3.5 that you call after a write in an existing job. The runtime jar declares Spark, Hadoop, Hudi, Iceberg and Delta as `provided`, so it uses the libraries already on the cluster. XTable has been in the Apache Incubator since February 2024, so it isn’t yet a top-level Apache project, and its latest release is 0.4.0-incubating.
strengths: Metadata-only: a sync writes a few metadata files and leaves the Parquet data alone, so one copy of the data serves Delta, Iceberg and Hudi readers
Omni-directional: any supported format can be the source and any other the target, so a Hudi or Delta writer can feed an Iceberg-only engine and the other way round
Incremental sync that falls back to a full sync by itself and tracks its own watermark, which the docs say makes it safe to call after every write
Pluggable sources and targets through a common table model, which is how Paimon and plain Parquet sources were added in 0.4.0
limits: Only copy-on-write and read-optimized views are synced: Hudi log files and Delta or Iceberg deletion vectors don’t carry over, so targets don’t see updates and deletes that still live in those files

Format quirks need settings on the source: Iceberg targets may need Parquet field ids (Delta column mapping, a Hudi extension), Hudi targets need Hudi 0.14 or later with the metadata table on, and Delta generated columns aren’t synced
Still incubating at version 0.x: releases are source-only, the `RunSync` jar must be built from source, and the Spark runtime jar brings none of the format libraries with it
Plain Parquet sources take the schema from the most recently modified file and can’t handle schema changes across files or partition columns that exist only in directory names

story: By 2023 the lakehouse had three popular table formats, Apache Hudi, Apache Iceberg and Delta Lake, and engines and cloud services each supported some of them. A table written in one format could be locked out of an engine that read another. All three store their rows in Parquet files, though, and differ only in the metadata layer.

In February 2023 Onehouse announced OneTable and invited others to help build bridges between the formats. Microsoft and Google joined, and after months of work on a prototype, Kyle Weller and Tim Brown announced on 15 November 2023 that OneTable was open source. It wasn’t a new table format, they wrote, but a converter that turns Hudi, Delta and Iceberg metadata into each other “in an omni-directional way”, with no data copied.

The same post announced a plan to donate it to the Apache Software Foundation. The proposal listed initial committers from Onehouse, Microsoft, Google, Walmart, Adobe, Cloudera and Dremio, and planned to rename the code from OneTable to XTable. XTable entered the Apache Incubator on 11 February 2024. Its first Apache release, 0.1.0-incubating, came out in August 2024, catalog sync arrived in 0.3.0 in June 2025, and Paimon and Parquet sources in 0.4.0 in August 2026.

choices.why: The three formats share Parquet as the data layer, so converting only the metadata makes the same files readable as all three, with “very little performance overhead” according to the launch post.

choices.choice: A common in-memory model with source and target interfaces
choices.why: Each format only needs a reader into the model and a writer out of it. The launch post used a Paimon source as the example of how the project could grow, and 0.4.0 added one.

The launch post said users could start from any format, convert to any other and round-trip across them in any combination, which also reassured users who need only one format that their tables were future-proof.
The launch post said the project’s success depended on it being neutral and governed by strong community principles, and announced the plan to submit it to the Apache Incubator to make sure of that.
